turns.t: Doctor, my neighbour here, Mr Hughes, can't hear properly and can't see well, and he's hardly going out anymore. I'm worried about him.
Thank you for bringing him in. Mr Hughes, how are you finding your hearing?
What? You'll have to speak up.
Your hearing, Mr Hughes. Is it giving you trouble?
Aye, I can't follow the telly, and on the phone it's just noise.
He turns the television up so loud that the whole street can hear it.
And your eyes?
Everything's blurry, especially reading. I can't read the paper anymore.
When did you start noticing these changes?
Och, I couldn't tell you. It crept up. A couple of years, maybe.
I only noticed this past winter, but I think it was going on before.
Do you go out and meet friends?
Not much now. I get lost in the conversation, so I don't bother.
He used to go to the bowls club every Thursday, and he stopped last spring.
That sounds lonely. How's your mood, Mr Hughes? ~
I'm all right. Just tired of missing things. ~
Do you have any medical problems?
He has high blood pressure, diabetes, and cataracts in the left eye, I think.
Let me check your pressure and pulse. ~
Aye, go on.
Blood pressure 146 over 84, pulse 72, temperature 36.5, oxygen 97 percent.
Is that all right? ~
A little high, but fine for his age. Now I'd like to look in your ears, Mr Hughes. ~
Go on.
There's a lot of wax in both ears, blocking the eardrums.
Wax? Is that why I can't hear? ~
It may be a big part of it. I'd like to have it removed and then recheck your hearing.
Can we do that here? ~
The nurse can arrange ear syringing next week, and I'll refer him for an eye test and a hearing test after.
I'll bring him. ~
In the meantime, I'd like him to have an eye test with the optician.
I'll book it for this month. ~
And I'd encourage him to go back to the bowls club once he can hear again.
Aye, maybe I will. ~
If he gets sudden hearing loss or severe dizziness, call us straight away.
I will. Thank you, doctor. ~
